summary: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a compact data format, and COSE defines how to sign, authenticate and encrypt data in it, plus how to represent cryptographic keys in CBOR. This document gives the structures and processing rules. Together with RFC 9053 it obsoletes RFC 8152.

eli5.summary: Think of a tiny sealed envelope for small gadgets. COSE tells devices how to sign and lock short messages so they stay safe while using very little space.

subtitle: The message formats for signing, MACing and encrypting CBOR data, and for writing cryptographic keys in CBOR.

tldr.problem: Small, constrained devices use CBOR as their compact data format, but CBOR had no standard way to sign, authenticate or encrypt data, or to carry cryptographic keys.
tldr.mechanism: COSE defines CBOR array structures for signed, MACed and encrypted messages, each with protected and unprotected header buckets, plus a key format. It also defines the exact byte strings that get signed, MACed or used as authenticated data.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9052 is an Internet Standard (STD 96). Together with RFC 9053 it obsoletes RFC 8152, and RFC 9338 updates it.

facts.label: Common header labels
facts.value: 1 to 6 (alg, crit, content type, kid, IV, Partial IV)

today: RFC 9052 is an Internet Standard (STD 96). It obsoletes RFC 8152 and, together with RFC 9053, replaces it. It has been updated by RFC 9338.

sections.title: Why COSE Exists
sections.content:
Constrained devices in the Internet of Things use CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) to encode data. It was designed for small code size and small messages. COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption) does for CBOR what the JOSE documents (such as JSON Web Signature and JSON Web Encryption) do for JSON: it defines how to sign, authenticate with a message authentication code (MAC), and encrypt data, and how to encode keys. It keeps the flavor of JOSE but is not a direct copy. For example, binary data is encoded directly instead of being base64-encoded.

This document defines the CBOR objects sent on the wire, the procedures for building the inputs to the cryptographic functions, and a set of header attributes. It does not define the use of specific cryptographic algorithms; an initial set is in RFC 9053, and RSA algorithms are in RFC 8230.

COSE was first designed to help secure Constrained RESTful Environments, but it can be used wherever one would consider JOSE or Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). Like those, it is only for store-and-forward or offline protocols. Using it in an online protocol that needs encryption requires an online key establishment step first. The RFC also deliberately leaves out a digest structure, because different protocols will want different fields around the digest value.
sections.eli5: Tiny gadgets send each other very short messages. COSE is a set of rules for putting a signature or a lock on such a message without making it much bigger.

sections.title: The Basic COSE Structure
sections.content:
Every COSE message is a CBOR array, and the first three elements are always the same: the protected header parameters (encoded and wrapped in a byte string), the unprotected header parameters (a map), and the content, which is either the plaintext or the ciphertext. The content can be detached, meaning it travels separately. Then the position holds a nil value. What follows depends on the message type.

There are six top-level message types, two each for signing, encryption and MACs. The single-party forms (COSE_Sign1, COSE_Encrypt0, COSE_Mac0) are used when the key is implicitly known. The other forms carry signatures or recipient structures.

A message can be identified by context, by a CBOR tag, by the cose-type parameter of the application/cose media type (REQUIRED for untagged messages), or by a CoAP Content-Format. COSE uses layers to separate concerns. For example, COSE_Encrypt has a content layer holding the encrypted plaintext and a recipient layer holding the encrypted content encryption key (CEK) for each recipient.
sections.eli5: Every COSE message is a list with the same first three slots: the notes that are sealed, the notes that are not, and the main content. The rest of the list depends on what kind of message it is.

sections.title: Header Parameters
sections.content:
COSE keeps two buckets of information about the content, algorithm or key. The protected bucket is cryptographically protected. The unprotected bucket is not. Both are CBOR maps keyed by a label (an integer or text string; the RFC uses the word label to avoid confusion with cryptographic keys). Both are required in every security object.

The protected map is CBOR-encoded and wrapped in a byte string, so that it travels unchanged. Senders SHOULD encode an empty protected map as a zero-length byte string rather than as a map. Labels MUST be unique, and a message with a repeated label MUST be rejected as malformed. If a parameter appears in both buckets, the protected one wins.

Common parameters are alg, crit, content type, kid, IV and Partial IV. The alg parameter MUST be authenticated where the ability exists. The crit parameter lists protected parameters that a receiver MUST understand, and it MUST be in the protected bucket. The kid value is only a hint and need not be unique, so it can sit in the unprotected bucket. The message IV is formed by left-padding the Partial IV with zeros to the IV length and XORing it with the Context IV.
sections.eli5: There are two sticky-note piles. One pile is sealed with a tamper sticker, so changes would be noticed. The other is open. Important notes, such as which lock was used, go in the sealed pile.

sections.title: Signing Objects and How Signatures Are Computed
sections.content:
COSE_Sign carries one or more signatures on the same content. Each signature is a COSE_Signature with its own protected and unprotected buckets. A message can, for example, carry both an EdDSA and an ECDSA signature so that a recipient can check whichever it supports. COSE_Sign1 is for a single signer and keeps all parameters in one pair of buckets. The two cannot be converted into each other, because the signature computation includes which structure is in use.

A signature is not computed over the message as sent. Instead, a canonical byte string is built from a Sig_structure array: a context string (Signature or Signature1), the body protected bucket, the signer protected bucket (omitted for COSE_Sign1), the externally supplied data and the payload. That array is CBOR-encoded to give ToBeSigned, which is passed to the signature algorithm.

Externally supplied data lets an application authenticate data that is not in the COSE object, such as CoAP options. The application must define how the byte string is built so that different inputs cannot produce the same bytes, the order is fixed, and both sides get the same result. A verifier must also check that the key belongs to the signing identity and that the identity is authorized.
sections.eli5: Before signing, COSE writes a standard checklist of everything that matters, in a fixed order, and signs the checklist. Change anything on it later and the signature no longer fits.

sections.title: Encryption and MAC Objects
sections.content:
For encryption, COSE_Encrypt0 is used when the key is known implicitly, with no recipient structure. COSE_Encrypt is used otherwise, including multiple recipients. It holds the ciphertext and an array of COSE_recipient structures, each holding an encrypted key and information about how it was protected. The same techniques and nearly the same structure are used for encrypting content and keys. This differs from CMS and JWE.

COSE restricts content encryption to algorithms that authenticate both the content and additional data (AEAD). The additional authenticated data is the encoding of an Enc_structure holding a context string (such as Encrypt0 or Encrypt), the protected bucket and the external data. For Authenticated Encryption (AE) algorithms without associated data, such as key wrap, the protected bucket MUST be zero length and no external data may be supplied.

MAC objects work alike. COSE_Mac0 is for an implicit key and COSE_Mac adds recipients. The MAC is computed over a MAC_structure with a context string (MAC or MAC0), the protected bucket, the external data and the payload. A MAC can confirm that content was unchanged. If the key comes from a preshared secret or Static-Static key agreement, it can also show who sent it, but it cannot prove the sender's identity to a third party.
sections.eli5: An encrypted message is a locked box whose lock also notices tampering. A MAC is a seal that only people who know the secret can make or check.

sections.title: Keys and Content Key Distribution
sections.content:
A COSE_Key is a CBOR map, and a COSE_KeySet is an array of keys that MUST contain at least one. The required element is kty (label 1). Other common parameters are kid, alg, key_ops and Base IV. If a key in a set is malformed or not understood, it is ignored and the others are processed normally. When a key has an alg, the application MUST check it matches the algorithm in use. The key_ops values (such as sign, verify, encrypt, decrypt and MAC create) restrict what a key may be used for.

For encrypted and MACed messages there are several ways to deliver the content encryption key to each recipient. Direct uses a shared secret as the key, or derives it, and must be the only mode used on the message. Key wrap encrypts a random CEK under a shared key, and the RFC considers it better than direct if the system can generate random keys. Key transport uses the recipient's public key. Direct key agreement derives the key with Diffie-Hellman and a KDF, and the message MUST have only one recipient. Key agreement with key wrap combines agreement with wrapping, so it suits several recipients. A password class is also listed, but no password algorithms have been defined.

Because COSE is for store-and-forward use, the receiver cannot supply fresh key material, so forward secrecy is not achievable with the key agreement methods here.
sections.eli5: To share a secret key you can hand over a key you already share, put the new key in a box locked with a shared key, or use the receiver's public lock. COSE supports all of these.

sections.title: Encoding Rules and Application Profiles
sections.content:
Signing and MAC computations need identical bytes on both sides, so the structures that feed them (the Sig_structure, Enc_structure and MAC_structure) have encoding restrictions aligned with the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements of RFC 8949. Encoding MUST use definite lengths and the shortest possible argument length. For example, the integer 1 is encoded as 0x01 and not 0x1801. Applications MUST NOT generate or process a map that uses the same label twice.

COSE gives security services but does not set algorithm requirements. Each application should define a profile. That profile picks which message types it uses, which header parameters, how external data is encoded, which algorithms are mandatory to implement, and how algorithms are negotiated or discovered. The RFC suggests choosing algorithms of different construction for a mandatory pair, such as HMAC-SHA512 and AES-CMAC. It points to RFC 8613 as an example profile.
sections.eli5: When two people check a signature, their checklists must be written the same way letter for letter. So COSE sets strict writing rules, and each app adds its own rules about which tools to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations need to protect private key material. The RFC highlights several points. Using the same key for two different algorithms can leak information about the key, so keys should be restricted to one algorithm, and the key type should be checked too (do not use an EC2 key where an OKP key is expected). Combining the direct recipient mode with another recipient exposes the direct key to the second recipient, which is why direct must be the only mode. Several algorithms in RFC 9053 limit how many times a key can be used.

With ECDH or direct plus KDF and two recipients, the second recipient holds a CEK derived from material that gives weak proof of origin. It could build a message that the first recipient wrongly trusts as coming from the original sender. Adding a key wrap step removes that issue.

Before acting on a message, an application must make a trust decision about the key: what the key owner is allowed to do, whether the algorithm is acceptable, whether key restrictions were checked, and whether any crit requirements were enforced. COSE gives no uniform padding, so message length can reveal content (an observer can tell YES from NO). Applications are responsible for padding.
sections.eli5: Do not use one key for many jobs, and always ask whether the sender is allowed to ask for this. Short and long messages look different, so apps should pad them if the length would give the secret away.

viz.caption: THE SIG_STRUCTURE THAT IS SIGNED (CDDL FROM RFC 9052)

data.title: Sig_structure
data.code:
Sig_structure = [
    context : "Signature" / "Signature1",
    body_protected : empty_or_serialized_map,
    ? sign_protected : empty_or_serialized_map,
    external_aad : bstr,
    payload : bstr
]
